Lessons.Title: Ways to Look at Quadrilaterals
ExplanationParagraphs:
Learning goal: You will classify quadrilaterals by the size of your angles, the length of your sides, and the presence of parallel and perpendicular sides.
In the previous lesson, you sorted and analyzed triangles by your sides and angles and began to form general statements about the properties of triangles. (Triangles always have three sides and angles, may have a right angle or equal sides, may be foldable into equal halves, never contain more than one obtuse angle, and so on.) In this lesson, you identify and sort quadrilaterals based on your angles and sides, including whether your sides are parallel. You are introduced to the term parallelogram to describe quadrilaterals with two pairs of parallel sides, but you are not expected to use this term throughout the unit.

2021 source lesson activities: Warm-up: How Many Do You See: Brick Pattern (10 minutes); Activity 1: Quadrilateral Hunt (20 minutes); Activity 2: What’s True about These Quadrilaterals? (15 minutes); Activity 3: Guess Again [OPTIONAL] (10 minutes); Cool-down: Quadrilaterals Rule (5 minutes)
Source-goal geometric reasoning: Classify quadrilaterals using parallel sides, right angles and equal side lengths, not their orientation.

Edulytics worked explanation: A quadrilateral has four sides; identify parallel or perpendicular pairs on each original card. Test whether right angles are present and which sides have equal lengths. A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus, meeting the required properties of each.
First-party Edulytics Cool-down (not gated original): Explain why every square is also a rectangle.
Original student diagrams, teacher card sorting, paper folding, and physical drawings require figure-by-figure / teacher validation.
